Its alt, "Festival returns with half-term activities and fun for all ages", is the headline of the story, the same text as the h3 link right after it. claimTrue: the alt states the news (a festival returning with half-term activities) rather than the puppets and puppeteer the photo shows, so the sentence holds of the capture. Skeptic's reason against the finding: the image is not a link; it is the teaser photo of a news card and its alt repeats the h3 headline link that follows it in the same article. Read as the photo's purpose in a teaser (to illustrate and identify the story), the headline arguably serves that purpose, and the only defect is redundancy with the adjacent headline, which many auditors treat as advisory. Others would call the photo informative and require the alt to say what it shows (the claim's point), and others would call it decorative and want alt="" (F38's test fails a purely decorative img with a non-null alt, a defect the claim, which implies a description is needed, does not name). Competent auditors would reasonably disagree about whether the element fails 1.1.1 and on what ground, so the label is uncertain although my answers lean to a pass. captureDiffers: the live page fetched on 2026-11-25 serves the same server-rendered with the same alt, and the screenshot shows the teaser photos rendered (the consent dialog and a repeated sticky header overlay parts of the stitched screenshot, and some snapshot bounds have height 0, but none of that touches the alt text), so no difference matters here.
